To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
O-isotope exchange among the fine-grained fractions of detrital quartz, clay minerals, and pore water is extensive at temperatures below 100 °C, but is less extensive at temperatures above 100 °C.

1) O-isotope exchange is more extensive between fine-grained clay minerals and pore water than between coarser-grained clay minerals or quartz and pore water; 2) the extent of O-isotope exchange increases with increasing temperature of burial; 3) quartz that forms diogenetically as an accomponiment to conversion of smectic to illite layers of the mixed-layer clay attains isotopic equilibration with the pore water, whereas detrital quartz does not.

the O-isotope ratios of shales are not equilibrated with those of their constituent minerals, that O-isotope exchange becomes more extensive with increasing temperature, and that O-isotope geotemperatures calculated from the isotope ratios of coexisting fine-grain quartz and clay are in good agreement with measured temperatures at temperatures up to 180 °C.

The main takeaway from our work is that
O-isotope exchange occurs between clay minerals and pore water in diagenetically altered shale.

O-isotope geothermal gradients calculated from O-isotope fractionation of quartz and clay are reasonable for temperatures up to at least 120 °C and that O-isotope fraction of coexisting quartz and clay can be used to calculate maximum burial temperatures for shales in the range of temperatures for which the method is valid.
O-isotope geothermal gradients in sedimentary sequences can be calculated by using O-isotope ratios of fine-grained quartz.
